name: Spartan education and the subordination of the individual to the state
plain_explanation: From birth, Spartans were shaped entirely to serve the state as soldiers: weak infants were exposed, boys were removed from home at seven for harsh communal training, and adult life remained highly regimented, with almost no personal liberty or private culture.
precise_definition: The Spartan system of state-controlled upbringing (agoge), combining physical hardening, minimal formal 'learning' beyond obedience and endurance, and lifelong subordination of private life to military and civic duty, extending in modified form to the physical training of girls.
why_it_mattered: This is the clearest institutional ancestor of the rigorous, state-directed education Plato prescribes for his guardians in the Republic, including the equal physical training of women.
historical_origin: Legendarily instituted by Lycurgus; described at length by Plutarch and criticized by Aristotle.
examples: Boys trained from age seven in a single school, taught obedience, endurance of pain, and combat rather than 'cultural or scientific education.'
Girls given the same physical (gymnastic) training as boys, including exercising naked alongside them.
Deformed or sickly infants examined and, if judged unfit, exposed.
objections: Aristotle argues the system failed even on its own terms, since Spartan women, exempted from the same discipline, lived in 'intemperance and luxury' and gained excessive influence.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates Plato's Utopian education of the guardian class (covered in the next chapter), and was invoked approvingly by later admirers from Rousseau to the architects of Nazi ideology, per Russell.
